title: Mycorrhizal inoculation enhances productivity, mineral nutrition, pomology, and bioactive compounds of sweet cherry under field conditions on calcareous soils
summary: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are increasingly recognized as a sustainable biological approach to improve nutrient acquisition and fruit quality in horticultural crops. Their role is particularly important under calcareous soil conditi
content: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are increasingly recognized as a sustainable biological approach to improve nutrient acquisition and fruit quality in horticultural crops. Their role is particularly important under calcareous soil conditions where nutrient availability is restricted, thereby reducing reliance on intensive chemical fertilization. This study evaluated the effects of AMF inoculation on root colonization, yield, mineral composition, pomological traits, and fruit biochemical composition of two sweet cherry cultivars (‘0900 Ziraat’ and ‘Sweetheart’) under field conditions. Mycorrhizal inoculation significantly increased root colonization compared to non-inoculated trees (from 54.35% to 95.05%). Fruit mineral concentrations increased under AMF treatment, particularly nitrogen (+ 26.9%), phosphorus (+ 18.9%), potassium (+ 19.1%), calcium (+ 26.1%), and magnesium (+ 12.1%). Main pomological (fruit weight, fruit width, fruit length) and biochemical characteristics (soluble solid content, titratable acidity, and pH) were not significantly affected, whereas functional bioactive compounds were markedly enhanced, including total phenolics (+ 13.9%), total anthocyanins (+ 10.8%), vitamin C (+ 18.1%), and antioxidant activity (+ 15.8%). Principal component analysis separated inoculated and non-inoculated treatments. It also showed that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi inoculation was associated with higher yield, mineral accumulation, and bioactive compound levels. Obtained results demonstrate how AMF inoculation increases yield without altering pomological traits while simultaneously promoting biochemical enrichment, thereby enhancing the nutraceutical quality of sweet cherry under calcareous soil conditions.

title: Water Usage and Environmental Impact of Data Centers: Sustainability Challenges and Pathways for Developing Countries
summary: The rapid global expansion of cloud computing and artificial intelligence has transformed data centers into critical infrastructure, but this growth carries a largely underappreciated environmental cost: intensive freshwater consumption. Th
content: The rapid global expansion of cloud computing and artificial intelligence has transformed data centers into critical infrastructure, but this growth carries a largely underappreciated environmental cost: intensive freshwater consumption. This paper presents a structured review of the water usage and environmental impact of data centers, emphasizing sustainability challenges facing developing countries. Drawing on peer-reviewed research, operator disclosures, industry efficiency metrics, documented community disputes across Latin America and Asia, and comparative regulatory experience from Ireland, the Netherlands, and Singapore, the paper synthesizes evidence on how evaporative cooling systems withdraw billions of litres of freshwater annually, with demand increasingly concentrated in water-stressed regions. The review finds that hyperscale operators have made measurable efficiency gains, yet absolute consumption continues to rise as AI workloads expand; that developing economies face a distinct risk profile shaped by weak water governance and limited disclosure requirements; and that unmanaged siting decisions have already triggered community opposition, legal challenges, and project delays in Chile, Uruguay, and Mexico. The paper proposes an integrated sustainability framework spanning technological measures (liquid and immersion cooling, closed-loop systems, non-potable water reuse), regulatory measures (mandatory water disclosure, water-risk-informed siting, water-positive licensing, and lessons from developed-market moratoria), and communityoriented measures (stakeholder consultation, benefit-sharing). It further examines the economic trade-offs developing-country policymakers face between investment attraction and resource protection. The paper concludes that reconciling digital infrastructure growth with water security in developing countries requires coordinated action from technology firms, regulators, and local communities, and outlines a research agenda for context-specific, empirically grounded policy design.

title: Technology qualification plan for very large wind turbine blades
summary: As wind turbines scale beyond 15 MW and blades exceed 100 m in length, ensuring structural integrity and operational reliability becomes increasingly complex. Accelerated development cycles and intensifying global market competition, driven
tags: Failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis
content: As wind turbines scale beyond 15 MW and blades exceed 100 m in length, ensuring structural integrity and operational reliability becomes increasingly complex. Accelerated development cycles and intensifying global market competition, driven by the emergence of new turbine manufacturers and design concepts, particularly from outside Europe, further heighten the need for systematic, risk-informed technology qualification (TQ). These trends introduce uncertainty by compressing the time available for design validation and by requiring project bids to be made on the basis of turbine models that may still be under development, often with unproven performance or limited field data. This paper presents a comprehensive TQ methodology for very large wind turbine blades, integrating a full Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) with a tailored qualification plan aligned to DNV-RP-A203. The FMECA identifies both conventional and scale-induced failure modes, with a particular focus on leading edge erosion, spar cap failure, adhesive debonding, lightning damage, and, aeroelastic and flow-induced instabilities. Each high- and very-high-risk failure mode is mapped to specific qualification activities - such as simulation, laboratory testing, field trials, and in-service monitoring - creating a traceable risk mitigation pathway. The study serves as a reference for future blade developments, incorporating cross-sector insights from aerospace, offshore energy, and nuclear qualification practices to strengthen the methodology. Through focusing qualification efforts on the most critical risks and combining model-based analysis with targeted physical evidence, the proposed framework supports faster, safer certification of next-generation rotor technologies, enabling confident deployment of ultra-large blades in a competitive, rapidly evolving global wind energy market.

title: Can Large-Scale Thermal Energy Storage Exploit the Effects of Renewable Generation on Wholesale Electricity Prices?
summary: Abstract Purpose of Review Electricity systems are experiencing increased penetrations of renewable generation. Because such resources have low, zero, or ( e . g ., due to policy choices) negative marginal costs, wholesale markets that oper
content: Abstract Purpose of Review Electricity systems are experiencing increased penetrations of renewable generation. Because such resources have low, zero, or ( e . g ., due to policy choices) negative marginal costs, wholesale markets that operate such systems yield an increasing number of time periods with low or negative prices. Contemporaneously, wholesale energy prices tend to remain high during time periods with limited renewable-generation availability. These price dynamics have the potential to embiggen the economic value of energy storage. This paper examines the potential value proposition of energy-storage technologies that can exploit these changing price patterns and dynamics. Recent Findings We focus on the value of thermal energy storage, which is a commercially viable and scalable energy-storage technology, that sees less deployment compared to electro-chemical energy storage. We find that thermal energy storage and electro-chemical energy storage are economically viable. Thermal energy storage has some technical characteristics, including sizing flexibility and synchronous inertia, which may make it preferable under some scenarios. Summary Changing price patterns and dynamics are likely to improve the economic rationale of energy-storage technologies. This includes technologies that are receiving attention, such as electro-chemical energy storage, and other technologies, such as thermal energy storage.

title: Modern approaches and future prospects in lettuce breeding for controlled environment agriculture
summary: Controlled environment agriculture (CEA) is expanding rapidly as a climate-resilient approach for year-round lettuce production near consumption centers. However, despite its supply chain advantages and high productivity, the economic viabi
content: Controlled environment agriculture (CEA) is expanding rapidly as a climate-resilient approach for year-round lettuce production near consumption centers. However, despite its supply chain advantages and high productivity, the economic viability and scalability of CEA-grown lettuce remain constrained by the continued reliance on cultivars developed for variable open-field conditions rather than stable, high-input, and space-limited environments of indoor production systems. This mismatch between existing germplasm and CEA-specific production requirements represents a critical gap that has not been comprehensively addressed in lettuce breeding. This review discusses the need for a paradigm shift in breeding priorities toward cultivars specifically optimized for CEA, with an emphasis on traits that improve output per unit of energy, time, and growing area. Key breeding targets include accelerated growth and shortened crop cycles, enhanced light-use efficiency and photosynthetic performance, improved tolerance to temperature extremes, compact plant architecture for high-density production, optimized shoot-to-root biomass partitioning for hydroponic systems, and resilience to major CEA-associated physiological disorders, pests, and diseases. Because CEA reduces many field-related stressors, breeding efforts can place greater emphasis on consumer- and market-oriented traits, including consistent product quality, enhanced nutritional value, and uniformity compatible with automated production systems. This review consolidates dispersed evidence on these CEA-targeted traits and links them to a modern lettuce breeding toolbox, providing a framework to guide cultivar development for controlled environments. We outline how integrating approaches ranging from conventional genetics and marker-assisted selection to genomic selection and gene-editing technologies such as CRISPR can accelerate genetic gain for these complex trait combinations. Furthermore, the integration of high-throughput phenotyping, artificial intelligence, and multi-omics platforms offers a powerful, data-driven approach to decipher genotype-by-environment interactions and optimize lettuce for controlled environments. By identifying critical knowledge gaps and outlining a targeted breeding framework, this review provides a roadmap for developing resource-efficient, high-performing, quality-focused lettuce cultivars tailored to next-generation CEA, thereby improving the industry’s profitability, sustainability and ability to meet the food demands of a rapidly urbanizing global population.

title: Effect of Fiber Dosage and Age on Creep Failure of Alkali-Activated Slag Concrete Under High Stress Sustained Loading
source: International Journal of Concrete Structures and Materials
summary: Alkali-activated slag (AAS) has emerged as a sustainable alternative to Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC), offering a viable pathway for mitigating global environmental footprints. However, its widespread structural application is often hinder
content: Alkali-activated slag (AAS) has emerged as a sustainable alternative to Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC), offering a viable pathway for mitigating global environmental footprints. However, its widespread structural application is often hindered by pronounced time-dependent creep deformation, particularly nonlinear creep under high sustained stress, which precipitates progressive internal damage and potential structural failure. While fiber reinforcement is recognized for enhancing concrete ductility, its specific role in modulating the high-stress creep behavior of AAS systems remains insufficiently explored. This study experimentally investigates the creep failure characteristics of Polypropylene (PP) fiber-reinforced AAS concrete, scrutinizing the coupled effects of fiber dosage, loading age, and stress intensity. Failure mechanisms were characterized via a multi-scale analysis incorporating failure patterns, creep coefficients, apparent lateral strain ratios, ultrasonic non-destructive testing, and crack morphology. Results indicate that fiber reinforcement fundamentally modifies the creep failure kinetics. Specifically, fibers actively constrain lateral expansion, reducing the apparent lateral strain ratio by up to 34% at failure, thereby transitioning the failure mode from brittle fracture to a pseudo-ductile yielding. The efficiency of the fibers is highly age-dependent. While improvements are marginal at 1 day, at 28 days under a critical 0.95 f c stress level, a 1.0% fiber dosage yielded a 156% increase in creep lifetime. These findings demonstrate that fiber inclusion provides a critical safety margin and mechanical redundancy for AAS concrete subjected to sustained high loads.

title: Cradle-to-Gate LCA of Fly Ash Mortar for Low-Carbon Construction: GWP Reduction, Uncertainty Analysis, and Policy Relevance
summary: This study has four objectives, namely 1) to quantify the cradle-to-gate Global Warming Potential (GWP) of mortar produced with 0%, 30%, and 50% fly ash substitution; 2) to identify the dominant emission contributors across material product
content: This study has four objectives, namely 1) to quantify the cradle-to-gate Global Warming Potential (GWP) of mortar produced with 0%, 30%, and 50% fly ash substitution; 2) to identify the dominant emission contributors across material production, transport, and mixing; 3) to evaluate uncertainty and sensitivity in the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) model; and 4) to interpret the mitigation potential in relation to Indonesia’s sustainable-construction and climate-policy context. This study was designed as a scenario-based cradle-to-gate LCA to quantify and compare the GWP of mortar mixtures incorporating fly ash. The functional unit was defined as 1 m3 of mortar targeted to an approximately 25 MPa compressive-strength class; however, the 30% and 50% fly ash mixtures were treated strictly as modelled LCA scenarios rather than experimentally validated mortar formulations. The system boundary was cradle-to-gate, covering raw material production, material transport to the batching plant, and mortar mixing. Fly ash was modelled using a cut-off allocation approach. A Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations was conducted for the 30% fly ash scenario. The baseline mortar without fly ash substitution generated the highest GWP, at 266.6 kg CO2-eq/m3. Replacing 30% of cement with fly ash reduced the GWP to 190.8 kg CO2-eq/m3, corresponding to a reduction of 75.8 kg CO2-eq/m3 or 28.4% relative to the baseline. A higher substitution level of 50% fly ash further reduced the GWP to 140.2 kg CO2-eq/m3, equivalent to a reduction of 126.4 kg CO2-eq/m3 or 47.4%. Overall, the scenario results indicate that fly ash mortar can be a promising low-carbon material option, but the findings should not be interpreted as proof of mechanical equivalence, and practical implementation requires compressive-strength verification, fly ash quality assessment, durability testing, site-specific transport data, plant-specific cement emission factors, and measured mixing-energy data.

title: Grounding groundwater: Spatialities of dispossession in the Kaveri Delta, India
summary: Abstract Groundwater degradation is commonly understood to exacerbate societal inequities. However, its effects can be more complex, reconfiguring existing patterns of advantage and disadvantage rather than simply intensifying them. This pa
content: Abstract Groundwater degradation is commonly understood to exacerbate societal inequities. However, its effects can be more complex, reconfiguring existing patterns of advantage and disadvantage rather than simply intensifying them. This paper applies political ecology and socio-hydrogeology to enquire how groundwater change in India’s Kaveri Delta manifests through the understandings and actions of government officials and farmers, and examine its societal implications. The research is set in a deltaic village dotted with tubewells for year-round paddy cultivation. Here, it combines aquifer mapping and monitoring conducted alongside farmers, with a spatial and qualitative analysis of landholding, water access, cropping patterns and livelihood options, in relation to caste. Aquifer monitoring uncovers recent groundwater salinisation, and the subsequent analysis reveals concomitant water dispossession, where the delta elite have accumulated the benefits of government-incentivised intensive agriculture, to the detriment of other farmers now contending with saline groundwater. However, the spatial heterogeneity of groundwater salinisation falls outside the socio-spatial patterns of caste-based inequity, as some middle caste farmers, in areas with recent groundwater salinisation, face agricultural losses and fare worse than Dalit (marginalised caste) farmers in areas retaining fresh groundwater. The analysis thus reveals 'spatialities of dispossession', where the processes and outcomes of dispossession are mediated by the spatial properties and relations associated with resource change (here spatially uneven groundwater salinisation). This can upend previous societal relations through changing geographies of resource access. Grounding groundwater socio-hydrogeologically, by attending to its dynamic materiality, spatiality and politics, the paper thus unravels its shared agency in shaping relations of inequity.

title: Financial and environmental evaluation of Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system upgrades for energy transition in Northern Germany
summary: The energy consumption of buildings and facilities significantly contributes to carbon emissions, highlighting the crucial role of efficient Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems in the energy transition. This paper eval
content: The energy consumption of buildings and facilities significantly contributes to carbon emissions, highlighting the crucial role of efficient Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems in the energy transition. This paper evaluates and discusses the financial feasibility and environmental benefits of upgrading a heating system based on waste-to-energy district heat. The study compares an obsolete system with an upgraded system using the same technology and to a fully electrified heat pump. The comparison is made using the Equivalent Annual Cost (EAC) and the carbon emission intensity (kg CO2e/m2). We demonstrate that a heat pump would potentially reduce carbon emissions by 56% but with an annual cost 15.6% higher in comparison to the actual water-to-air system. Upgrading the actual system to a new and more efficient one has potential for reducing carbon emissions by around 45% with similar costs to the heat pump option. It is highlighted that the option for using a heat pump has potential to reduce carbon emissions, as is pointed out in the scientific literature, but it is still not financially attractive for customers to quit the old systems. Results justify the development of policies to stimulate the substitution of obsolete heating systems with incentives to make it financially attractive for the customers.

title: Forging agrarian trajectories through assets, strategies, and values: structural hybridization between agro-extractivism and the socio-biodiversity economy in the Brazilian Amazon
summary: Abstract The socio-biodiversity economy is widely regarded as an alternative agrarian pathway to agro-extractivism in the Brazilian Amazon, capable of reconciling conservation, social inclusion, and income generation. Recent research challe
content: Abstract The socio-biodiversity economy is widely regarded as an alternative agrarian pathway to agro-extractivism in the Brazilian Amazon, capable of reconciling conservation, social inclusion, and income generation. Recent research challenges this promise. Agro-extractivist dynamics have been documented in socio-biodiversity markets, while the farming households that sustain this economy remain largely overlooked, and often idealized. This study examines the livelihood configurations and agrarian trajectories of two groups of cocoa farmers in the Transamazon region—one organic, one conventional—affiliated with two regional cooperatives. It adopts a mixed-method design that extends the Sustainable Livelihoods Approach beyond its traditional focus on material assets by integrating values as a key dimension of livelihood strategies. Data were gathered between March and September 2024 through structured questionnaires, semi-structured interviews, and ethnographic observations. Findings show historically produced asset asymmetries between the two groups, alongside a shared condition as petty commodity producers. Divergent agrarian trajectories emerge not only from material conditions but also from the interplay between assets and the values that guide how farmers mobilize their resources. Conventional farmers pursue emancipation from commodity dependence through economic diversification and market upgrading, while their cooperative channels individual pragmatism toward place-based value aggregation. Organic farmers secure their livelihoods through agroecological farming, but their cooperative operates from a weaker position that hinders the translation of these values into economic practice. Both these trajectories reveal the entanglement of agro-extractivist and socio-biodiversity dynamics within the same households, a condition this study terms structural hybridization. More broadly, the study calls for greater analytical attention to the agrarian dynamics unfolding among the smallholders who sustain the socio-biodiversity economy.

title: PFAS alternatieven: Marktkansen in Nederland
summary: Dit rapport analyseert de rol van PFAS in twee belangrijke Nederlandse sectoren en in één productgroep (halfgeleiders, elektrolysers en brandblusschuimen) en verkent kansrijke alternatieven in het licht van strengere regelgeving. Het biedt
content: Dit rapport analyseert de rol van PFAS in twee belangrijke Nederlandse sectoren en in één productgroep (halfgeleiders, elektrolysers en brandblusschuimen) en verkent kansrijke alternatieven in het licht van strengere regelgeving. Het biedt inzicht in toepassingen, beschikbare alternatieven, transitiepaden en investeringskansen om zowel de PFAS-transitie als de concurrentiekracht van Nederland te versterken.

title: Sustainable Board Governance, Corporate Social Responsibility Fulfillment, and Differences in ESG Information Disclosure: A Comparative Case Study of Conch Cement and Qingsong Jianhua Co., Ltd.
summary: Under the background of the deepening concept of sustainable development, the ESG framework has put forward important requirements for the green governance of high-emission and heavily polluting industries. Based on the governance practice
content: Under the background of the deepening concept of sustainable development, the ESG framework has put forward important requirements for the green governance of high-emission and heavily polluting industries. Based on the governance practice of two cement-listed enterprises with the same state-owned holdings and the same regulatory environment, this study explores the transmission path from sustainable board governance to corporate ESG performance. By analyzing the practical differences of enterprises in the three levels of governance structure setting, responsibility implementation results and information disclosure quality under the ESG framework, we clarify the core role of the green decision-making mechanism of the board of directors in environmental responsibility and the fulfillment of social responsibility, and deeply analyze the real problems such as structural deficiencies, insufficient incentives, and non-standardized disclosure practices in the current ESG development of heavily polluting state-owned enterprises. Subsequently, targeted countermeasures were put forward, such as improving the internal governance system, developing innovative green decision-making mechanisms, adjusting the assessment incentive mechanism, strengthening mandatory requirements for ESG disclosure, and improving the professional ability of directors, so as to promote the green and sustainable development of heavily polluting enterprises. Finally, summarize the research conclusions and emphasize that the achievement of ESG goals by heavily polluting enterprises requires the coordination of internal governance and external supervision.

title: TRI HITA KARANA: THE KEY TO SUSTAINABLE TOURISM AND CONSERVATION AT GUNUNG KAWI TEMPLE IN GIANYAR REGENCY, BALI, INDONESIA
summary: This study aims to develop and evaluate a strategic model for sustainable tourism grounded in the Balinese philosophy of Tri Hita Karana. Hita Karana is a strategy to maintain a balance between tourism and conservation. This study uses qual
content: This study aims to develop and evaluate a strategic model for sustainable tourism grounded in the Balinese philosophy of Tri Hita Karana. Hita Karana is a strategy to maintain a balance between tourism and conservation. This study uses qualitative research methods. This study is located in Tampaksiring Village, Gianyar Regency, Bali. Informants include community leaders, managers of the Gunung Kawi Cliff Temple site, village officials, and visiting tourists. Data collection was conducted through interviews, observations, and documentation. Data analysis in this study used the interactive model of Miles and Huberman, which comprises three main steps: data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing/verification. The CHGF model synchronises the government's role as an institutional anchor for spatial planning (Palemahan), the community's role as guardians of intrinsic cultural values (Pawongan), and the private sector's role as a catalyst for ethical innovation. This model does not eliminate the sanctity (Parahyangan) or structural integrity of the site. Therefore, this mod el is oriented toward high-value conservation to maintain a dynamic balance between 21st-century prosperity and 11th-century preservation. This study concludes that the sustainability of tourism at Pura Tebing Gunung Kawi fundamentally depends on the successful implementation of the Collaborative Heritage Governance Framework (CHGF), grounded in the Tri Hita Karana philosophy. The CHGF model explains that, in the modern era, preserving Pura Tebing Gunung Kawi requires integrating policies, market innovations, and social capital in line with Bali's characteristics.

title: Promoting synergies and mitigating trade-offs: governance conditions in climate action and SDG interactions
summary: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) represent an indivisible agenda in which interactions among goals—synergies and trade-offs—must be managed. While substantial progress has been made in quantitative modeling and network analysis of S
content: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) represent an indivisible agenda in which interactions among goals—synergies and trade-offs—must be managed. While substantial progress has been made in quantitative modeling and network analysis of SDG interactions, systematic evidence drawn from empirical policy cases remains limited, leaving a persistent knowledge gap between theoretical analysis and on-the-ground practice. This study screened 128 empirical case study papers cited in Chapter 3.4 of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) Synthesis Report (SYR), which addresses long-term interactions among adaptation, mitigation, and sustainable development. Papers were classified into five domains—energy and power; land use, forests, and agriculture; urban, transport, waste, and local governance; industry, supply chains, and circular economy; and governance—and systematically analyzed for synergies, trade-offs, enabling factors, and remaining challenges. Findings indicate that synergies consistently arise not from single measures but from cross-sectoral policy integration, long-term institutional frameworks, multi-criteria assessment, inclusive stakeholder engagement, and aligned incentive structures. Trade-offs, by contrast, were consistently associated with institutional fragmentation, asymmetric power and resource distribution, short-termism, and incoherent policy mixes rather than appearing as inevitable outcomes. Five key driving forces for synergy promotion and trade-off mitigation were identified: policy objective integration, inclusive governance and redistribution of agency, long-term vision and time horizon reorientation, incentive structure redesign, and institutional capacity for learning and adaptation. This study advances the literature by moving beyond descriptive mapping of SDG interactions to a mechanism-oriented analysis that explains how policy design and governance arrangements shape or mitigate these interactions in practice. These findings suggest that the most impactful leverage points reside in deep systemic properties—governance structures, decision-making rules, and dominant development paradigms—rather than in isolated technical or policy interventions, and that strategic combinations of shallow and deep interventions are required to enhance both effectiveness and political feasibility in SDG implementation.

title: Pine Honey as a Distinct Functional Honeydew Product with Unique Composition, Bioactivity and Sustainability
summary: Pine honey, a distinctive honey produced primarily in Mediterranean regions, particularly in Türkiye, is a beekeeping product with notable compositional and biological properties. Unlike flower honeys derived from nectar, pine honey origina
content: Pine honey, a distinctive honey produced primarily in Mediterranean regions, particularly in Türkiye, is a beekeeping product with notable compositional and biological properties. Unlike flower honeys derived from nectar, pine honey originates from the secretions of insects – primarily the species Marchalina hellenica – that feed on the sap secreted by pine trees (Pinus brutia and Pinus nigra). This distinct origin leads to a chemical profile that differs significantly from other types of nectar-based honeys. Pine honey is characterized by low levels of simple sugars, high electrical conductivity, and high mineral content, combined with a rich array of phenolic compounds and bioactive components. This composition contributes to its significant biological activities, including antioxidant, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects. Compared with floral honeys, pine honey exhibits greater stability and a distinct functional profile, making it a promising candidate for health-related applications. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of pine honey, focusing particularly on its compositional uniqueness, physicochemical properties, and biological characteristics. Comparative aspects between pine honey and flower honeys are given special emphasis; key differences in sugar profile, enzyme activity, mineral composition, and bioactive compounds are highlighted. Additionally, to provide a deeper understanding of the quality and authenticity of pine honey, recent advances in analytical techniques for its characterization, such as chromatographic and spectroscopic methods, are discussed. Bringing together the latest scientific knowledge, this section aims to highlight the functional importance of pine honey, its potential as a natural bioactive product in nutrition and health, and its contribution to sustainable beekeeping and ecosystem management.

title: Dietary substitution of fish oil with plant oils in juvenile black sea trout Salmo labrax (Actinopterygii, Salmoniformes, Salmonidae): Implications for growth, lipid metabolism, and tissue fatty acid quality
summary: Global fish oil production has plateaued while salmonid aquaculture expands, creating urgent demand for sustainable alternative lipid sources. This study evaluated the effects of replacing dietary fish oil with canola oil, safflower oil, an
content: Global fish oil production has plateaued while salmonid aquaculture expands, creating urgent demand for sustainable alternative lipid sources. This study evaluated the effects of replacing dietary fish oil with canola oil, safflower oil, and their blends on growth performance, feed utilization, condition indices, and muscle fatty acid composition in juvenile Black Sea trout, Salmo labrax Pallas, 1814. Seven isonitrogenous and isolipidic diets (45% crude protein, 18% crude lipid) differing only in lipid source—fish oil (FO), safflower oil (SO), canola oil (CO), and their 50:50 binary and equal ternary blends—were fed to triplicate groups of juvenile Black Sea trout (initial weight 30.22 ± 0.19 g) for 90 days. Growth performance, feed utilization, condition indices, and fatty acid compositions of diets and white dorsal muscle were determined. Growth performance and feed utilization did not differ significantly among treatments ( P > 0.05), confirming that complete fish oil replacement did not compromise growth performance. However, significant differences were observed in fat deposition rate, viscerosomatic index, and hepatosomatic index ( P < 0.05). Muscle fatty acid profiles closely mirrored dietary composition: saturated and n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (EPA, DHA) declined while monounsaturated and n-6 fatty acids increased with increasing plant oil inclusion. The muscle n-3/n-6 ratio fell most sharply in the safflower oil group. Economic analysis revealed that complete plant oil substitution reduced feed costs by 12%–13% compared to the fish oil control. Both canola and safflower oils can effectively replace fish oil in Black Sea trout diets without compromising growth. Canola oil emerges as the more broadly balanced substitute, while safflower oil’s strong n-6 enrichment restricts its suitability to blended or finishing strategies.

title: The politics of climate change and urban agriculture in South Africa
summary: Urban agriculture has increasingly gained global recognition as a strategic approach for simultaneously addressing food security and climate change through mitigation and adaptation interventions. However, its potential remains constrained
content: Urban agriculture has increasingly gained global recognition as a strategic approach for simultaneously addressing food security and climate change through mitigation and adaptation interventions. However, its potential remains constrained in South Africa, where climate change exacerbates the country’s persistent challenges of food insecurity, poverty, unemployment, inequality, and the triple burden of malnutrition. The study explored the politics of climate change mitigation and adaptation measures for urban agriculture in South Africa. It also identified the fragmentation of related policies and programmes, and the factors that contributed to it. The article examines the nature, causes, and consequences of policy fragmentation by drawing on the available literature. The study systematically reviewed the literature using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. The review used multiple electronic databases, including Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science, to maximise the retrieval of relevant studies and minimise publication bias. The findings reveal that the separation of climate, agriculture, food security, and urban development governance has resulted in systemic governance failures that hinder policy coherence, resource allocation, and implementation capacity. The study concludes that South Africa will not realise the transformative potential of urban agriculture for climate change mitigation, adaptation, and sustainable food systems unless it shifts from fragmented, sector-specific governance to integrated, coherent, and multi-level policy approaches that recognise the interdependence of climate action, food systems, and urban development. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge by providing the first comprehensive synthesis of governance fragmentation affecting climate-responsive urban agriculture in South Africa. It also offers evidence-based recommendations for strengthening policy integration, institutional coordination, and adaptive governance.

title: Prim-Lex Theory in Energy Transition: A CLL Early Warning Index for Identifying Tipping Points under Nine-Dimensional Phase-Coherence Governance ——An Empirical Study Based on IEA 2026, IRENA 2026, IGCC 2026, and IMF 2026 Data
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The global energy transition stands at a historic threshold, crossing from the "fossil fuel era" to the "renewable energy era." According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) World Energy Investment 2026 report, global energy investment
content: The global energy transition stands at a historic threshold, crossing from the "fossil fuel era" to the "renewable energy era." According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) World Energy Investment 2026 report, global energy investment is projected to reach USD 3.4 trillion in 2026, with clean energy investment at approximately USD 2.2 trillion (64.7% of total investment) and fossil fuel investment at approximately USD 1.2 trillion. More urgently, according to the Global Carbon Project and the fourth edition of the Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC), the remaining carbon budget for the 1.5°C target has fallen to about 130 Gt CO₂, which at current emission rates would be exhausted in approximately 3–4 years. Meanwhile, the IMF estimates that global fossil fuel subsidies amount to about USD 7 trillion per year, which is 23 times the annual climate finance commitments. As a reference, the IMF reports that the current global average carbon price is only about USD 3 per tonne, while IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has explicitly stated that the global average carbon price needs to reach above USD 75 per tonne by 2030 to generate sufficient mitigation incentives. In other words, the current global carbon price is only about 4% of the target level, while the scale of fossil fuel subsidies (USD 7 trillion/year) is 2.5 times the potential global carbon tax revenue (USD 75/t × 37 Gt CO₂ ≈ USD 2.8 trillion/year). This dual failure of "price signal vacuum" and "subsidy distortion" is precisely the deep institutional cause of the rapid depletion of the global carbon budget (130 Gt CO₂) within 3–4 years. However, coal investment has paradoxically risen to USD 180 billion (the highest since 2012), and natural gas investment reached USD 330 billion (the highest in nearly a decade), forming a complex pattern of "parallel expansion of old and new energy." Meanwhile, the fourth edition of the Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC) report shows that in early 2026, the remaining global carbon budget (for the 1.5°C target) was only 130 Gt CO₂, which would be exhausted in about 3–4 years at current emission rates. The global energy system is in a "critical zone" of transition from one steady state to another——neither a stable continuation of the old order nor a full establishment of the new order. Based on the complete theoretical system of Prim‑Lex Theory (Economic Climatology)——the Fivefold Prim‑Fire as its ontological foundation, the three‑tier constraints (GC⁴A) as hard boundaries, the Five‑Element dynamic coupling equations as the core of system dynamics, the Eight‑Dimensional Framework as the diagnostic coordinate system, and Prim‑Nexus Guidance as the directional anchor——this paper, for the first time, systematically applies the CLL (Capital Market Condensation Level) phase‑transition early warning model to energy transition pathway planning. This paper elaborates, dimension by dimension, the calculation principles and data collection

title: Fracture resistance of screw-retained premolar crowns fabricated with pressed lithium disilicate glass-ceramic and CAD-CAM translucent zirconia
source: Brazilian journal of oral sciences/Brazilian Journal of Oral Sciences
summary: CAD-CAM translucent zirconia materials have been marketed to fabricate fixed definitive prostheses. However, comparison of their fracture resistance to conventional pressed lithium disilicate glass-ceramic as screw-retained, implant-support
content: CAD-CAM translucent zirconia materials have been marketed to fabricate fixed definitive prostheses. However, comparison of their fracture resistance to conventional pressed lithium disilicate glass-ceramic as screw-retained, implant-supported crowns is limited. Aim: This in vitro study evaluated the fracture resistance of screw-retained premolar crowns fabricated from pressed lithium disilicate glass-ceramic and CAD-CAM translucent zirconia materials. Methods: Forty premolar crowns (n=10) were fabricated from three CAD-CAM translucent zirconia materials (Katana Zirconia STML, Zolid FX Multilayer, and NexxZr Multi+) and from 1 lithium disilicate glass-ceramic (IPS e.max Press). Each crown was luted to titanium abutments with a standard platform and 3-mm gingival height. The abutments were screwed onto 4.3-diameter x 11.5-length titanium implants. All specimens underwent thermal aging (30000 cycles at 5 ºC and 55 ºC with a 20-second dwell time) and mechanical fatigue (600,000 cycles at 2 Hz with a 80-N axial load). The fracture load was applied at 45 degrees to the long axis of the implant until failure. Results: No specimens fractured during thermal aging or mechanical fatigue. No significant differences were found between the groups (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.172). The mean fracture loads varied between 1278.02 N and 1696.65 N. All fractures originated in the occlusal-screw access opening and extended to the cervical area. Conclusion: CAD-CAM translucent zirconia materials and the pressed lithium disilicate glass-ceramic showed comparable resistance when used for screw-retained crowns cemented on prefabricated titanium abutments.

title: Multidimensional factors influencing young farmers’ willingness to attend agricultural training in rural China
summary: In agricultural modernization, improving the skills of young farmers is crucial, but the willingness to participate in training in underdeveloped areas is still low. To this end, based on 1467 survey data from a rural area, this study used
content: In agricultural modernization, improving the skills of young farmers is crucial, but the willingness to participate in training in underdeveloped areas is still low. To this end, based on 1467 survey data from a rural area, this study used a binary Logistic model to analyze the determinants of training participation from four dimensions: personal, economic, social and psychological. The results showed that gender and education level significantly affected the willingness to participate in training ( p < 0.05); farmers with high family income had low willingness to participate in training ( p < 0.05), while being willing to pay higher training fees significantly enhanced the willingness to participate in training ( p < 0.01); social support had a positive effect on the willingness to participate in training ( p < 0.05); motivation to participate in training and confidence in future development significantly affected the willingness to participate in training ( p < 0.01). Heterogeneous analysis shows that low-income groups are more dependent on training costs and social support, while high-income groups are more influenced by personal planning and expectations. The study reveals the multidimensional mechanism of young farmers ‘training decision-making, emphasizing the pertinence and effectiveness of training policies by lowering economic threshold and strengthening support system.

title: Influence of Ethanol, Methanol and N-Hexane Extracts of Kigelia Africana Leaves and Fruits on Oxidative and Biochemical Properties in Induced Diabetic Rats
source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HEALTH AND PHARMACEUTICAL RESEARCH
summary: Diabetes mellitus is a common metabolic disorder characterized by sustained hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and disrupted biochemical parameters. This study investigated the effects of ethanol, methanol, and n-hexane extracts from the leav
content: Diabetes mellitus is a common metabolic disorder characterized by sustained hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and disrupted biochemical parameters. This study investigated the effects of ethanol, methanol, and n-hexane extracts from the leaves and fruits of Kigelia africana on oxidative and biochemical markers in alloxan-induced diabetic rats. The plant materials were extracted using maceration and solvent evaporation methods. Diabetes was induced by a single intraperitoneal dose of alloxan monohydrate. Experimental groups included normal controls, diabetic controls, and treatment groups receiving graded doses of the extracts. Key parameters measured were fasting blood glucose, antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase [SOD], catalase [CAT]), reduced glutathione (GSH), malondialdehyde (MDA), liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP), and lipid profiles. Alloxan increased blood glucose by about 69%. Treatment with Kigelia africana extracts reduced glucose levels by 45–62%, with methanol leaf extract being most effective (62% reduction). Antioxidant markers improved significantly: SOD and CAT activities increased by 55–70%, MDA decreased by ~58%, and GSH rose by 60%. Liver enzymes decreased by 40–55%, indicating hepatoprotection. Lipid profiles improved with 35–50% reductions in total cholesterol and LDL, and a 30% increase in HDL. Methanol and ethanol extract outperformed n-hexane, suggesting polar solvents extract more bioactive antidiabetic compounds. The study concludes Kigelia africana exhibits strong antidiabetic, antioxidant, and hepatoprotective effects, supporting its traditional use in diabetes management.
