title: Digital communication and narrative governance in BRICS healthcare: a website media analysis of public hospital vision and mission statements
source: Scientific Electronic Library Online (Scientific Electronic Library Online)
summary: Abstract: This study conducts a qualitative thematic analysis of vision and mission statements from leading publicly listed hospitals in BRICS countries-Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa-to explore institutional health prioriti
content: Abstract: This study conducts a qualitative thematic analysis of vision and mission statements from leading publicly listed hospitals in BRICS countries-Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa-to explore institutional health priorities and strategic orientations. Drawing on official data from top-ranked government hospitals, the analysis identifies recurring the-matic commitments and their relative emphasis across national contexts. Using a structured coding framework and frequency analysis, seventeen core themes were initially extracted and then consolidated into major thematic groups, such as Medical Care/Services, Governance & Administration, Patient Focus, Education & Research, and Service Commitment. Radar dia-grams and comparative tables were employed to visualize cross-national similarities and divergences. Findings reveal that each country exhibits distinct institutional priorities: South Africa emphasizes Service Commitment (43.2%), China highlights Administration (27%), Russia focuses on Medical Care (23.6%), Brazil prioritizes Excellence (13.79%), and India centers on general Hospital identity (10%). While shared attention to quality, public health, and governance is evident, significant gaps persist in themes such as Community Engagement, Access & Affordability, and Ethics & Humanization. These disparities underscore the influence of political, historical, and structural factors on how healthcare institutions define and communicate their purpose. The study contributes to the emerging field of narrative health governance by demonstrating that institutional language is both symbolic and strategic. Vision and mission statements are not merely rhetorical but actively shape organizational identity and public expectations. The results offer valuable implications for health policymakers, administrators, and global health scholars aiming to align institutional narratives with universal health coverage, equity, and sustainable development goals. Future research is encouraged to link these thematic commitments with hospital performance metrics and extend the framework to non-BRICS countries for a more globalized understanding.

title: Clean Development as a Global Polycrisis Response Strategy
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Clean Development is presented as a unified, macro‑strategic framework capable of resolving the structurally entangled crises now defining the global polycrisis. As the monograph states, “the international community has entered an era defin
content: Clean Development is presented as a unified, macro‑strategic framework capable of resolving the structurally entangled crises now defining the global polycrisis. As the monograph states, “the international community has entered an era defined by… a condition in which multiple, structurally entangled global crises interact such that their combined impact far exceeds the sum of each crisis in isolation.” The work argues that climate destabilization, sovereign debt distress, fossil‑fuel price volatility, food system fragility, and geopolitical fragmentation form a synchronous shock architecture that overwhelms traditional siloed governance. Clean Development is advanced as the only strategy capable of simultaneously expanding economic growth, accelerating decarbonization, stabilizing macro‑financial systems, and strengthening human development. The monograph demonstrates that fossil‑dependent development models now generate the very shocks that suppress growth—via foreign‑exchange drain, debt overhang, and climate‑induced asset destruction. Clean energy, decentralized electrification, and green industrial policy instead create self‑reinforcing macroeconomic multipliers: reducing WACC‑driven capital cost penalties, eliminating fuel import liabilities, expanding fiscal space, and unlocking downstream mineral value chains worth 12× to 54× more than raw ore exports. Empirical evidence across Chapters 1–12 shows that clean transitions deliver: Absolute decoupling of GDP growth from emissions, 2.5×–3× higher employment multipliers than fossil investments, Balance‑of‑payments stabilization through fuel displacement, Human capability expansion via decentralized energy access, Climate resilience through adaptation finance and statutory debt‑pause clauses, Industrial upgrading through domestic refining mandates and regional clean‑development archetypes. The monograph concludes with a Ten‑Year Global Clean Development Compact (2026–2036)—a coordinated sovereign roadmap integrating NDCs into fiscal plans, deploying a multilateral FX‑risk facility, tripling MDB concessional lending, mandating climate‑resilient debt clauses, and establishing green industrial compacts. Clean Development is positioned not as an environmental agenda but as the central macroeconomic strategy for achieving resilient, equitable prosperity across the Global South.

title: The Sustainable Urbanization Challenge Across the Global South
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: By 2050, cities across Sub‑Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America will absorb 2.5 billion new urban residents, representing 90% of global population growth. As the monograph states, this surge is unfolding under “cond
content: By 2050, cities across Sub‑Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America will absorb 2.5 billion new urban residents, representing 90% of global population growth. As the monograph states, this surge is unfolding under “conditions of severe municipal capital scarcity, infrastructure backlogs, and non-linear physical climate risks” . Rapid expansion is producing a compounding urban polycrisis: unplanned peripheral sprawl, expanding informal settlements, extreme heat domes, pluvial flash floods, coastal storm surges, and widening infrastructure deficits exceeding $3.2 trillion. The monograph argues that sustainable urbanization requires a decisive pivot from reactive crisis response to proactive, climate‑aligned urban design. Core interventions include Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) corridors, nature-based sponge city hydrology, distributed rooftop solar and district cooling, in‑situ informal settlement upgrading, and land value capture–enabled municipal finance. As the text emphasizes, “climate risk in the Global South is fundamentally a crisis of unserviced informal urbanization” . Across 12 analytical chapters, the monograph integrates empirical modeling, engineering standards, and fiscal instruments to construct a unified 2026–2050 roadmap. Key findings include: Compact urban form and high‑albedo materials can reduce microclimate heat anomalies by 6.8°C. High‑ambition TOD can raise clean transit mode share above 78% by 2050. Sponge city infrastructure reduces stormwater runoff by 85%, transforming flood risk into aquifer recharge. In‑situ slum upgrading costs 1/7th as much as peripheral relocation while dramatically improving service access. Modernized municipal finance—digital cadastres, green bonds, land value capture—can close 81% of the $2.8T climate infrastructure gap. The monograph concludes with a call for a Global South Sustainable Urban Compact, urging sovereign governments and multilateral institutions to commit 2% of annual GDP to subnational resilience and guarantee universal tenure and basic services by 2040. Sustainable urbanization, it argues, is not optional: it is the central civilizational requirement for ensuring human dignity, economic productivity, and climate stability for the next century.

title: Beyond adoption: How digital technologies build resilience among resource-constrained SMEs in a developing economy
source: The International Journal of Entrepreneurship and Innovation
summary: Despite growing interest in digital technology adoption among small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), limited research examines how adoption translates into business resilience in marginalised, resource-constrained settings in developin
content: Despite growing interest in digital technology adoption among small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), limited research examines how adoption translates into business resilience in marginalised, resource-constrained settings in developing economies. This study addresses that gap by examining the antecedents of digital technology adoption among marginalised SMEs in Ghana and how adoption builds business resilience. Drawing on the Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework and resilience theory, a quantitative cross-sectional survey was administered to 145 enterprise owners and managers in rural and peri-urban Ghana, with data analysed using PLS-SEM. Results indicate that customer pressure and entrepreneurial orientation significantly and positively influence SMEs’ behavioural intention to adopt digital technologies, whereas perceived usefulness, technological complexity, internal digital skills, and government policies do not have significant effects. Behavioural intention positively and significantly enhances business resilience. Additionally, business size and longevity moderate some adoption relationships, highlighting the influence of contextual enterprise characteristics. This study contributes to the current body of knowledge by first extending the TOE framework by incorporating business resilience as a measurable post-adoption outcome. Second, the study provides empirical evidence from a marginalised enterprise context in sub-Saharan Africa and finally, the study introduces business size and longevity as moderating variables.

title: The Climate Adaptation Infrastructure Gap Across Emerging Economies
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Emerging and developing economies are entering an era where physical capital formation no longer occurs against stable climatic baselines. Instead, intensifying thermal extremes, hydrological volatility, and cyclonic hazards are eroding inf
content: Emerging and developing economies are entering an era where physical capital formation no longer occurs against stable climatic baselines. Instead, intensifying thermal extremes, hydrological volatility, and cyclonic hazards are eroding infrastructure lifecycles, suppressing productivity, and threatening long‑run income convergence. The monograph quantifies a $215–$387 billion annual adaptation financing gap, widening to $660 billion by 2040 and over $1.1 trillion by mid‑century, while tracked flows remain near $34 billion, leaving an 88% deficit. As the document states: “the annual adaptation financing requirement across developing countries currently stands between $215 billion and $387 billion… tracked international adaptation finance flows totaled approximately $34 billion annually in 2024.” Across water systems, power grids, transport corridors, urban drainage, coastal defenses, and agricultural value chains, the monograph demonstrates that resilient engineering premiums are modest (3–8%), yet lifecycle benefit‑cost ratios exceed 4:1, reaching 7.8:1 for stormwater systems and 5.8:1 for water storage. Failure to close this gap imposes a 0.45–0.85 percentage‑point annual drag on TFP, locking vulnerable nations into low‑growth equilibrium traps. The work advances a comprehensive capital‑architecture framework: blended finance stacks, first‑loss multilateral guarantees, local‑currency hedging (TCX), parametric catastrophe bonds, green banks, and national resilient infrastructure pipelines. Sovereign fiscal stability is addressed through Climate Resilient Debt Clauses (CRDCs), which pause debt service for 24 months after disasters, preventing debt spirals triggered by contingent liability realization. The monograph concludes that adaptation is not an environmental concession but a macroeconomic growth strategy. Institutionalizing whole‑life procurement, basin‑scale hydrological storage, hardened power grids, climate‑proofed logistics, sponge‑city urban hydrology, nature‑based coastal armor, and distributed agricultural infrastructure can secure long‑run convergence, protecting trillions in exposed capital stock and enabling emerging economies to reach 42.5% of the OECD income frontier by 2050, compared to 18% under unmitigated climate drag.

title: Laser‐Induced Local De‐Doping in Organic Semiconductors
summary: ABSTRACT This study explores control of the doping level in organic semiconductor films using scanning continuous wave laser radiation. The feasibility of this one‐step non‐contact post‐deposition approach is explored for a benchmark materi
content: ABSTRACT This study explores control of the doping level in organic semiconductor films using scanning continuous wave laser radiation. The feasibility of this one‐step non‐contact post‐deposition approach is explored for a benchmark material system comprising the high‐mobility polymeric semiconductor PBTTT‐C14 p‐doped with the small‐molecular acceptor F 4 TCNQ. De‐doping is achieved via laser‐driven photothermal heating that induces neutralization and subsequent diffusion and/or sublimation of dopant molecules from the irradiated region. Comparison of 785 and 561 nm excitation, which are resonant with the absorption features of doped and neutral semiconductor, respectively, reveals that excitation at 785 nm leads to a less pronounced organic semiconductor degradation at comparable laser irradiance. Modulation of doping level is achieved with laser‐resolution‐limited feature sizes below 10 µm, with laser power adjustment enabling the tunability of electrical resistance by two and five orders of magnitude for excitation at 785 and 561 nm, respectively. This fully digital process is conducted in ambient atmosphere and does not require any additional equipment, therefore allowing straightforward integration with high‐throughput mass‐production of molecular electronics.

title: Climate Resilience as an Engine of Sustainable Economic Convergence
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Climate volatility has become the defining macroeconomic constraint of the twenty‑first century, fundamentally reshaping the prospects for growth and convergence across emerging economies. As the monograph states, “economic convergence betw
content: Climate volatility has become the defining macroeconomic constraint of the twenty‑first century, fundamentally reshaping the prospects for growth and convergence across emerging economies. As the monograph states, “economic convergence between emerging economies and advanced industrial nations is physically impossible without climate-resilient infrastructure” . Intensifying heat, hydrological extremes, and compound hazards now operate as non‑linear capital destruction shocks and severe Total Factor Productivity (TFP) drags, eroding physical assets, suppressing labor capacity, and widening long‑run income gaps. This work reframes climate adaptation not as a defensive environmental cost but as high‑yield productive capital essential for sustaining growth. Resilient infrastructure—hardened grids, elevated transport corridors, circular water systems, and decentralized agrarian technologies—extends asset lifespans, prevents catastrophic depreciation, and delivers lifecycle benefit‑cost ratios exceeding 4:1 across sectors. By protecting human capital from thermal stress, preserving industrial throughput, and stabilizing logistics networks, resilience generates a powerful TFP preservation wedge that restores productivity growth trajectories otherwise crippled by climate extremes. The monograph demonstrates that climate resilience also functions as a sovereign financial stabilizer. Vulnerable nations face climate‑related risk premia of 150–350 bps on sovereign bonds, constricting fiscal space and raising the cost of capital. Embedding statutory adaptation pipelines compresses spreads, protects credit ratings, and prevents debt spirals triggered by repeated disaster reconstruction. Innovative blended‑finance architectures—first‑loss concessional tranches, green investment banks, parametric risk transfer—unlock private capital at 4–8× leverage, enabling scalable national resilience investment. Across agriculture, water systems, urban agglomerations, and trade corridors, the analysis shows that resilience is the precondition for structural transformation: stabilizing food systems, securing industrial water supply, protecting urban labor productivity, and ensuring uninterrupted export logistics. Technology leapfrogging—AI early warning, nature‑based coastal hybrids, microgrid controllers—further accelerates convergence by enabling low‑cost, high‑efficiency climate defenses. The monograph concludes that national development strategies must institutionalize resilience through comprehensive National Resilience Frameworks (NRFs), integrating climate stress‑testing into public investment management, sovereign debt strategies, and sectoral industrial policy. As summarized in the text, “adaptation is the foundational high-yield productive infrastructure required to preserve physical capital, protect labor capacity, compress sovereign risk premia, and sustain long-run convergence” .

title: How attitudes and beliefs about abortion stigmatization shape access to safe abortion services among women in Nepal: a qualitative study
summary: Despite the legalization of abortion in Nepal in 2002 and the provision of free, safe abortion services (SAS) since 2016, significant barriers persist. This study explores the nature and extent of abortion stigma and its impact on access to
content: Despite the legalization of abortion in Nepal in 2002 and the provision of free, safe abortion services (SAS) since 2016, significant barriers persist. This study explores the nature and extent of abortion stigma and its impact on access to SAS, examining the beliefs and perceptions of key stakeholders in Nepal. A qualitative study was conducted in four districts (Jhapa, Gorkha, Parsa, Surkhet), representing diverse ecological regions and provinces. Data were collected through 20 in-depth interviews (IDIs) with post-abortive women (PAW), 5 key informant interviews (KIIs) with policy representatives, and 16 focus group discussions (FGDs) with community men and women. Purposive and snowball sampling were used. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis guided by the SABAS framework. Key findings indicate widespread lack of clarity about the legal status and availability of SAS. Abortion is highly stigmatized, perceived as immoral, sinful, and equivalent to “killing a child,” leading to guilt, social exclusion, and discrimination, particularly against unmarried women. Findings are organized around four stigma domains: internalized, enacted, perceived, and structural stigma. Stigma is perpetuated by community members, religious adherents, and patriarchal structures, creating barriers to safe access. Abortion stigma remains a profound barrier to realizing legal abortion rights in Nepal. Reducing stigma requires comprehensive strategies including education, provider training, and engaging men, religious leaders, and youth as advocates. Specific policy recommendations and future research directions are outlined.

title: Algorithmic fairness as a human–technology interaction problem
summary: Algorithms shape high-stakes decisions across society. While promising efficiency, algorithms also raise fairness concerns. This article proposes that algorithmic fairness is best understood as a human-technology interaction problem rather
content: Algorithms shape high-stakes decisions across society. While promising efficiency, algorithms also raise fairness concerns. This article proposes that algorithmic fairness is best understood as a human-technology interaction problem rather than a purely technical challenge. Algorithms can reproduce human biases, amplify them through feedback loops, or create new forms of unfairness through objectives, proxies, and seemingly neutral variables. Yet they can make decision processes more explicit, disparities more visible, and actively mitigate discrimination. Fairness depends not only on statistical properties but also on how algorithms are designed, used and experienced by those affected by their decisions. This article therefore offers an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates insights from social justice, psychology, computer science, judgment and decision-making, and management.

title: Employee Well-Being dalam Human Resource Management: Analisis Bibliometrik dan Pemetaan Ilmiah
summary: Employee well-being has become one of the strategic issues in Human Resource Management (HRM) due to its important role in enhancing organizational performance and sustainability. As the number of publications in this field continues to gro
content: Employee well-being has become one of the strategic issues in Human Resource Management (HRM) due to its important role in enhancing organizational performance and sustainability. As the number of publications in this field continues to grow, a comprehensive mapping is needed to understand research trends, the intellectual structure, and emerging themes. This study aims to map the development of employee well-being research in Human Resource Management using a bibliometric approach. The research data were obtained from 1,803 documents indexed in Scopus and analyzed through performance analysis and science mapping using VOSviewer software. The findings indicate that publications have increased significantly, particularly since 2018. The intellectual structure of the field is dominated by the themes of human resource management, job satisfaction, and burnout, while emerging themes include Green Human Resource Management, Sustainable Human Resource Management, personnel turnover, and mental health. These findings suggest that employee well-being research has evolved into a multidisciplinary field with an increasing focus on sustainability-related issues. This study contributes by mapping the development of the literature and providing a foundation for future research agendas and Human Resource Management practices.

title: The Effect of Sharia Financial Technology (Fintech) on Financial Inclusion from the Perspective of Islamic Economic Law
summary: Islamic fintech growth in Indonesia raises questions about the factors influencing financial inclusion through usefulness, ease of use, and the integration of a sharia compliance framework. This study aims to analyze the effects of perceive
content: Islamic fintech growth in Indonesia raises questions about the factors influencing financial inclusion through usefulness, ease of use, and the integration of a sharia compliance framework. This study aims to analyze the effects of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and sharia compliance on financial inclusion in Indonesia. A quantitative method was used, with online questionnaires distributed to 150 purposively selected Islamic fintech users in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS 26, with validity, reliability, and classical assumptions assessed. The study found that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and sharia compliance all have positive and significant effects on financial inclusion in Indonesia. Individually, perceived usefulness shows ? = 0.312 (p < 0.001), ease of use shows ? = 0.276, and sharia compliance shows ? = 0.358. Simultaneously, the variables significantly influence financial inclusion with F = 68.412 and p < 0.001. Adjusted R² equals 0.576, indicating that 57.6 percent of the variance is explained by the predictors in the model. These findings confirm a strong model fit and demonstrate that sharia fintech enhances financial inclusion through ethical digital financial services within an Islamic framework. Perceived usefulness, ease of use, and sharia compliance significantly determine financial inclusion and support Islamic fintech development in the Indonesian context. This study provides implications for regulators, fintech operators, and DSN-MUI for enhancing the development of an inclusive, ethical, and compliant Islamic finance system.

title: Double Adjustable‐Loop Cortical Buttons for Minimally Invasive Anatomic Double‐Bundle Medial Patellofemoral Ligament Reconstruction
summary: Recurrent patellar dislocation is a common condition in young and active individuals, with medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) injury being the primary pathological factor in most cases. Anatomic double-bundle MPFL reconstruction has been
content: Recurrent patellar dislocation is a common condition in young and active individuals, with medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) injury being the primary pathological factor in most cases. Anatomic double-bundle MPFL reconstruction has been established as an effective treatment for patellar instability; however, the optimal fixation method remains a matter of debate. Conventional techniques often employ suture anchors and interference screws for patellar and femoral fixation, which may require larger medial incisions, compromise the extensor mechanism, and increase the risk of bone tunnel fracture or graft laceration because of screw divergence. To overcome these limitations, we describe an MPFL reconstruction technique using dual adjustable-loop cortical button fixation on both the femoral and patellar sides. This approach provides suspensory fixation with a minimal implant, preserves bone stock and soft-tissue integrity, and enables controlled graft tensioning under arthroscopic visualization. This technique represents an alternative to traditional anchor- or screw-based MPFL reconstruction methods.

title: Beyond Theoretical and Philosophical Debates: The Imperatives of Dependency Theory and Appreciating the Development Quagmire in Africa
source: Journal of Arts and Sociological Research
summary: This study delves into the practical implications of Dependency Theory in addressing Africa's development challenges, moving beyond theoretical and philosophical debates to explore the tangible imperatives that arise from this critical pers
content: This study delves into the practical implications of Dependency Theory in addressing Africa's development challenges, moving beyond theoretical and philosophical debates to explore the tangible imperatives that arise from this critical perspective. Dependency Theory highlights the unequal power dynamics between developed and developing countries, emphasizing how patterns of economic exploitation and unequal exchange perpetuate underdevelopment in Africa. By considering the development quagmire in Africa, characterized by historical legacies, structural constraints, and external influences, this study underscores the urgency of adopting a Dependency Theory lens to inform development strategies on the continent. Through a nuanced analysis of Dependency Theory's insights, this study seeks to illuminate the importance of prioritizing self-reliance, reducing external dependence, and fostering inclusive development approaches in Africa. By bridging theory and practice, this study aims to contribute to a more informed and effective discourse on addressing Africa's development challenges within the context of Dependency Theory.

title: Observation to Openness: Governing Hydrological Data in a Non-Stationary World
source: Digital Presentation and Preservation of Cultural and Scientific Heritage
summary: The movement from observation to openness has become a defining challenge in environmental sciences. This challenge is particularly acute for hydrological governance in a non-stationary world. The assumptions underpinning water management,
content: The movement from observation to openness has become a defining challenge in environmental sciences. This challenge is particularly acute for hydrological governance in a non-stationary world. The assumptions underpinning water management, planning, and infrastructure design have been increasingly challenged by climatic variability, land-use change, and urbanization. These pressures have increased both the volume of environmental data produced and the strategic importance of governing that data effectively. However, hydrological data systems remain dispersed across institutions, scales, and jurisdictions. This paper argues that the transition from observation to openness is no longer a secondary technical reform but a core condition for water security, scientific reproducibility, risk governance, and equitable adaptation. Using a systems lens, it examines the full hydrological observation and data lifecycle and shows how bottlenecks at any stage can undermine decision-making. The paper then interrogates the quality-versus-quantity debate under conditions of non-stationarity, uncertainty, and the abundance of multi-source data, emphasizing that openness without metadata, standards, and accountability can reproduce rather than address epistemic weaknesses. A new governance paradigm is proposed, anchored in FAIR data principles, interoperability, public-value logic, and the doctrine of openness, as open as possible, and as closed as necessary. Particular attention is given to transboundary hydrology, data sovereignty, institutional asymmetries, and the growing need for trusted cross-border data flows. The paper concludes with a layered policy agenda for Member States, distinguishing what should, might, or can be done. Its central claim is that, in a non-stationary world, hydrological observation achieves full public value only when it is embedded in a culture of governed openness.

title: Toxicological evidence that methylmercury exposure amplifies bone destruction and systemic impact associated with apical periodontitis in rats
summary: This study investigated whether long-term methylmercury exposure aggravates apical periodontitis in Wistar rats. Thirty-two male rats (90 days old) were randomized into four groups (n = 8): control, methylmercury, apical periodontitis, and
content: This study investigated whether long-term methylmercury exposure aggravates apical periodontitis in Wistar rats. Thirty-two male rats (90 days old) were randomized into four groups (n = 8): control, methylmercury, apical periodontitis, and methylmercury + apical periodontitis. Methylmercury was administered daily by intragastric gavage (0.04 mg/kg/day) for 60 days, while apical periodontitis was induced on day 32 by pulp exposure to the oral cavity for 28 days. After euthanasia, total mercury levels and systemic oxidative stress markers were analyzed in blood; additionally, mandibles were evaluated for lesion volume and alveolar bone quality using micro-computed tomography and histological analysis. Data were analyzed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, followed by two-way ANOVA and Tukey's post hoc test (p < 0.05). The methylmercury + apical periodontitis group showed significantly larger periapical lesions and reduced alveolar bone quality compared to non-exposed animals (p < 0.05), with decreased trabecular thickness, lower bone volume/tissue volume ratio, and increased tissue destruction. Moreover, this group exhibited more intense oxidative alterations, including reduced antioxidant defenses (reduced glutathione and total antioxidant capacity equivalent to Trolox) and increased lipid peroxidation. Therefore, under the conditions of the present experimental model, long-term methylmercury exposure preceding and overlapping with apical periodontitis development resulted in increased lesion volume, impaired alveolar bone quality, and more pronounced systemic oxidative alterations, indicating an aggravation of apical periodontitis.
